catalog_quote: The syllabic canon of the Bibling languages is (C₁) V (C₂), where C₁ can be any consonant, most sequences of stop + resonant, or the sequence sl; where V can be any vowel; and where C₂ can be any consonant. Stress tends to be penultimate. Resonants in clusters after voiceless stops tend to be voiceless. ... Lmg pmarsek [pm̥ár̥sek] 'their father' In addition, all languages permit a word-initial syllabic nasal that never occurs with stress. ... Lmg mla [m̩lá] 'you go' Lmg ŋgo [ŋgó] 'he precedes' ... new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (402 pp, text; the PDF's metadata gives the author M.D. ROSS). Extracted pp. 262-265 with extracted text and rendered pp. 263-264 (printed pp. 253-254) at 150 dpi and read them visually. The quoted passage is present verbatim on printed p. 253 (§2 Phonology): "The syllabic canon of the Bibling languages is (C1) V (C2), where C1 can be any consonant, most sequences of stop + resonant, or the sequence sl; where V can be any vowel; and where C2 can be any consonant. Stress tends to be penultimate. Resonants in clusters after voiceless stops tend to be voiceless." and on p. 254: "In addition, all languages permit a word-initial syllabic nasal that never occurs with stress." The page-mapp…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is (as a tendency, not stated as exceptionless) on the penultimate syllable; a word-initial syllabic nasal never counts as a stress-bearing syllable, so in words like m̩lá 'you go' and ŋgó 'he precedes' the stress falls on the only full vowel. Supported by Thurston 1987 (PL B-99, p. 34) for all NW New Britain languages including Lamogai: 'for words pronounced in isolation, stress is usually penultimate in all languages'.
new_statements.exceptions: Stated only as a tendency ('tends to be'); word-initial syllabic nasals never carry stress. Thurston 1987 p. 34 adds that stress patterns in running speech 'have not been worked out in detail'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, citation/isolation forms; running-speech patterns explicitly unstudied (Thurston 1987:34). Statement is for the Bibling group jointly (Mouk, Aria, Tourai, Lamogai); Lamogai-specific data preliminary (Bulauatne village, 1982).
new_statements.identity_note: The deciding statement is made for "the Bibling languages" as a group (Mouk, Aria, Tourai = Mouk-Aria [mwh]; Lamogai, Rauto/Murien, Ivanga/Pulie = Lamogai [lmg]), not for Lamogai alone. Thurston's Lamogai data come from "a very short period of research in Bulauatne in 1982" and he asks that they "be treated as extremely preliminary" (p. 252); Rauto and Ivanga data are omitted. Lamogai examples on pp. 253-254 do carry penultimate stress marks (pmarsek [pm̥ár̥sek] 'their father', ino anak [inának] 'its pus', agu inoŋ [agúnoŋ] 'my neck', pupu ine [pupúne] 'his liver'; initial syllabic nasals unstressed: mla [m̩lá] 'you go', ŋgo [ŋgó] 'he precedes').
